messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 42

**Vignette: Rajan, Age 61**

Rajan has spent the better part of three decades working for a small non-profit organization that provides food security resources to immigrant communities in his city. He is the kind of man who arrives early and stays late, who knows the names of every volunteer's children, who finds genuine meaning in the slow, unglamorous work of helping people rebuild their lives in a new country. His colleagues describe him as steady and warm. He would have described himself that way too, until fourteen months ago.

It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Rajan was driving home from a community fundraising event, tired but satisfied, replaying the night in his mind. A driver running a red light struck his car at full speed on the passenger side. The impact spun the vehicle across two lanes of traffic. Rajan remembers the sound — a sound he says is impossible to describe to anyone who hasn't heard it — and then a strange, suspended silence before he understood that he was still alive. He sat in the wreckage for nearly twenty minutes before emergency services arrived, unable to move, certain at several points that he was dying. He sustained a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, and a serious concussion. The physical injuries healed within months. Everything else has not.

In the weeks following the accident, Rajan told his wife, Priya, that he simply needed rest. He minimized what had happened, partly because minimizing difficulty is something he has done all his life, and partly because he genuinely believed he would feel normal again soon. But normal did not come. He began waking at two or three in the morning, heart pounding, drenched in sweat, with the sensation of impact still reverberating through his body. The dreams were not always about the crash directly — sometimes he was simply trapped somewhere, unable to move, the world going dark around him.

Driving became impossible. For the first two months, he told himself it was practical caution. Then he admitted, quietly, that sitting behind the wheel made his chest close up and his hands shake in a way he could not control. He now takes the bus to work, which adds forty minutes to his commute each way, and he has constructed elaborate explanations for colleagues who ask why he no longer drives to site visits. He rides in cars when he must — when Priya insists on taking him to appointments — but he sits rigid in the passenger seat, watching every intersection with a vigilance that exhausts him.

At work, Rajan functions, but not as himself. He finds it difficult to concentrate during long meetings. He loses the thread of conversations. He has caught himself snapping at a young program coordinator over something trivial and felt a shame afterward that sat with him for days. The work that once felt like a calling now sometimes feels like a performance he is barely sustaining. He worries that people can see the difference in him, though no one has said so directly.

He has said very little to Priya about the depth of what he is experiencing. She knows he is not sleeping well. She does not know that some evenings, when he hears a loud noise from the street outside — a car backfiring, a dumpster lid slamming — he has to leave the room and stand in the hallway with his eyes closed, waiting for his body to believe it is safe. He does not want her to worry. He also, on some level, does not have the language for what is happening to him. Men of his generation, in his experience, were not taught that the mind could be injured the way the body can.

What brings him to therapy now is not a crisis but an accumulation — a slow recognition, finally named by his physician at a routine appointment, that what he is carrying has a shape and a name, and that carrying it alone is no longer working.
